title: Underwater salt mine closure in Ohio raises safety and supply concerns for winter
summary:
Questions remain about reason for leak, safety of drinking water and where salt can be sourced for roads during winter

When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton Salt mine in Ohio, the company had only one option: shut the mine down for good.

For locals in and around Fairport Harbor, it means the loss of 77 jobs; but for the wider region, which depends on its salt reserves to keep roads ice- and snow-free every winter, it could mean travel chaos.

Photograph: Alex Potemkin/Getty Images/iStockphoto Ohio Underwater salt mine closure in Ohio raises safety and supply concerns for winter Questions remain about reason for leak, safety of drinking water and where salt can be sourced for roads during winter Stephen Starr Sat 14 Nov 2026 08.00 EST Last modified on Sat 14 Nov 2026 08.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton Salt mine in Ohio , the company had only one option: shut the mine down for good. For locals in and around Fairport Harbor, it means the loss of 77 jobs; but for the wider region, which depends on its salt reserves to keep roads ice- and snow-free every winter, it could mean travel chaos. On top of that, in the weeks since the mine’s closure what’s been concerning mining experts and residents alike across the Great Lakes region is the mine’s location – about 2,000ft (610 meters) underneath Lake Erie. And that is sending broader warning signals across the region among activists and environmentalists, as to whether the issue could eventually hit other mines underneath the Great Lakes. At the Fairport Harbor facility, one of 12 rock salt mines that Morton Salt runs around the world, around 1.3 million tons of rock salt were mined from underneath the lake every year. The Trump administration wants underwater datacenters. One Great Lakes non-profit is already preparing Read more Last winter’s colder and snowier than average weather ate into road salt stockpiles at hundreds of municipalities across the region. Situated 30 miles (48km) from the now-shuttered mine, Trumbull county’s 200,000 residents relied entirely on the Fairport Harbor mine for road salt. Trumbull county’s location downwind of Lake Erie means its roads and highways are particularly affected by lake-effect snowstorms and the freeze-thaw process for up to five months a year. “We get about 30,000 tons [of salt] a year from the mine. But we have a stockpile of around 14,000 tons,” says David DeChristofaro, the Trumbull county engineer. “We are waiting for the Ohio department of transportation [to see about acquiring additional road salt supplies]. If necessary, we will mix salt with aggregate, one to one, as was typically done 15 years ago, to stretch our supply of salt. But that adds to cost because it needs to be swept up at the end of winter.” Trumbull county gets around 4.5ft (1.4 meters) of snowfall every winter. Authorities in a township in a neighboring county have had to issue a warning to motorists about potentially hazardous driving conditions this winter because of the salt shortage. While the mine closure could mean transportation problems for more than a million residents in a region of Ohio that experiences especially harsh winter conditions, the water intrusion has also raised safety questions. With five salt mines situated partly or entirely underneath Great Lakes waterways – in Fairport Harbor, Detroit and Cleveland, and two over the Canadian border in Ontario – a growing concern is that weeks later, Morton Salt officials say they still can’t find the source of the water intrusion. The salt is extracted by drilling and using explosives, and while the distance between the bed of Lake Erie and Morton’s Fairport Harbor mine is in excess of 1,000ft (305 meters), decades of blasting and the presence of underground aquifers could contribute to significant subterranean rock movement, say experts. “Blasting can fracture rock near an excavation, and removing rock changes the stresses carried by the roof, pillars and surrounding layers. For water to enter, there must also be a connected pathway from a water source to the mine,” says Xiong “Bill” Yu, a professor of engineering at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. “A nearby aquifer could supply that water through a fault, connected fractures, or a compromised shaft or seal.
